disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through learning of it occurring to close others. It is characterized by persistent intrusive recollections of the event, avoidance of trauma-related cues, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting more than one month and causing significant impairment. The clinical course can be acute or chronic, with onset often within three months of the trauma but sometimes delayed, and symptoms may fluctuate in intensity over time. PTSD is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the requirement of a qualifying traumatic event and the specific pattern of re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal linked to that event.

narrative.personality: Ernestine is a quiet, reflective, and compassionate planner who finds solace in solitary creative pursuits and nature along the Gulf Coast.
narrative.stressor: Ernestine’s PTSD began after she was driving back from a late evening grant-writing retreat and was caught in a sudden coastal storm, hydroplaned on a causeway near the Gulf wetlands, and was struck broadside by a speeding truck, leaving one child passenger in the other vehicle dead at the scene and Ernestine trapped in her car for nearly an hour. In the months that followed, she tried to return to her meticulous administrative routines and mindfulness practices, but the combination of guilt about surviving, graphic memories of the accident, and the legal depositions related to the crash steadily eroded her sense of safety and emotional connection to her work, her art, and even her family. Over the ensuing year and a half, she became increasingly withdrawn at home and at the early childhood center, delegating site visits and avoiding any travel near the water or driving at night, while forcing herself to maintain the appearance of competent fiscal and program leadership. As her inability to feel joy in painting, birdwatching, or time with her spouse persisted and began to jeopardize both her marriage and her effectiveness at work, she agreed—at her spouse’s urging and after a concerned colleague commented on how “numb” she seemed—to seek psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to feel any joy or warmth toward anything or anyone anymore.”

narrative.personality: Keisha is energetic, sociable, and competitive yet detail-oriented, pouring herself into community activities, church music, and her work at the library.
narrative.stressor: Keisha’s difficulties began when an armed robbery occurred at the Opa Locka Public Library one evening while she was closing up alone, during which a masked gunman forced her to lie on the floor at gunpoint while he emptied the cash box and threatened to kill her if she looked at his face. Although physically unharmed, she returned to work within a week, insisting on keeping the circulation desk running and reassuring others, but the fear associated with that night quietly intensified as she resumed late shifts, handled cash, and worked in the now-quiet building. Over the next year and seven months, she increasingly rearranged her schedule to avoid evenings, refused to participate in off-site outreach events near the site of the robber’s getaway, and gradually dropped out of some community festivals and line-dancing events held after dark, all while telling herself she was just “too busy” or “too old for the late nights.” When she found herself turning down a promotion that required supervising evening hours and realized she was driving blocks out of her way to avoid the library’s back entrance where the robber had cornered her, she finally confided in a church friend, who encouraged her to seek professional help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep going out of my way to avoid anything that reminds me of that robbery at the library.”

narrative.personality: Dianna is a practical, organized, and quietly generous person who enjoys learning, nature, and nurturing community connections through hobbies and volunteering.
narrative.stressor: Dianna’s PTSD developed after she suffered a sudden cardiac arrest while hiking with her husband; she collapsed on the trail, stopped breathing, and required prolonged CPR from a bystander and a chaotic emergency helicopter evacuation before being resuscitated in the hospital. Surviving what she experienced as coming close to death profoundly shook her previously steady, solution-focused outlook, and returning home did not bring the relief she expected, as everyday bodily sensations and environmental noises began to feel ominously tied to that day on the trail. Over the following 19 months, she forced herself to maintain her meticulous performance at the insurance office and her caregiving roles, yet the lingering fear associated with medical settings, emergency sirens, and even vigorous activity led her to abandon hiking groups, withdraw from some volunteer work, and avoid certain social gatherings where health scares were discussed. When her exaggerated reactions to small sounds—like dropped objects at work or ambulance sirens passing by—started to draw worried comments from coworkers and made it increasingly hard for her to participate in bridge games or book club meetings without embarrassment, she accepted a referral from her primary care physician for psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I jump out of my skin at the smallest noise, like something terrible is about to happen again.”
